stories.headline: Napoleon Solo Wins 151st Preakness Stakes at Laurel Park
stories.summary:
Napoleon Solo won the 151st Preakness Stakes on Saturday at Laurel Park in Maryland, holding off Iron Honor down the stretch for the colt's first victory of the year. The race was held at Laurel Park rather than the traditional Pimlico venue, which is currently undergoing renovation.

Kentucky Derby winner Golden Tempo did not enter the race, leaving an open field of 14 horses to contest the middle jewel of the Triple Crown. Napoleon Solo's victory means there will be no Triple Crown bid heading into the Belmont Stakes, as the Derby and Preakness were won by different horses.

stories.headline: U.S.-Nigeria Joint Strike Kills Senior Islamic State Leader in Lake Chad Basin
stories.summary:
U.S. and Nigerian forces killed Abu Bakr al-Mainuki, a senior Islamic State leader, in a precision air-land operation carried out early Saturday in the Lake Chad Basin. President Trump announced the strike in a late-night social media post, describing al-Mainuki as the group's global second-in-command and a key figure in IS financing and organization who had been plotting attacks against the United States and its interests. Nigerian President Bola Tinubu confirmed the operation, stating that al-Mainuki was killed alongside several of his lieutenants during a strike on his compound.

The Nigerian military task force spokesperson described the mission as a 'highly complex precision air-land operation' lasting three hours, conducted without casualties or loss of assets. Al-Mainuki, born in Nigeria's Borno province in 1982, took command of the IS branch in West Africa after his predecessor was killed in 2018 and was sanctioned by the U.S. in 2023. The UN has reported that IS intensified activity in West Africa, with more than 500 attacks recorded between January and October of last year.

Some analysts disputed Trump's characterization of al-Mainuki as the global second-in-command, though his importance to the West Africa affiliate was not in question. The operation is the latest under a security partnership between the U.S. and Nigeria that began last year. The task force called it 'the single most consequential counterterrorism outcome' in the region since operations began in 2015.

stories.headline: Update: Canadian Passenger from Hantavirus-Hit Cruise Ship Tests Positive, Raising Total Infections to 11
stories.summary:
A Canadian who sailed on the MV Hondius, the cruise ship struck by a hantavirus outbreak in April, has tested presumptive positive for the disease, British Columbia health officials announced Friday. The individual, one of four people isolating on Vancouver Island after disembarking in Canada, had developed mild symptoms. The case raises the total number of confirmed or presumptive infections to 11, all among passengers, with three deaths recorded — two confirmed to have had the virus.

British Columbia's senior health officer Dr. Bonnie Henry said the positive result still requires confirmation by a national microbiology lab, and stressed that none of the other five Canadians from the ship have tested positive. The six Canadian passengers are split between two couples isolating on Vancouver Island and two others self-isolating at their home in Ontario. The 21-day isolation period initially required of the Canadians may now be extended following the new positive result.

Health officials emphasized that hantavirus, particularly the Andes strain believed responsible for the ship outbreak, does not carry pandemic potential and differs fundamentally from respiratory viruses such as Covid or influenza. The cruise ship departed Argentina on April 1 and docked in Tenerife last week, allowing its 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries to begin isolation. The WHO has recommended 42 days of isolation for those exposed.

stories.headline: Texas Children's Hospital Agrees to Create First 'Detransition Clinic' and Fire Five Doctors in DOJ Settlement
stories.summary:
Texas Children's Hospital, the largest children's hospital in the United States, has agreed to establish what Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton called the country's 'first-ever detransition clinic' as part of a settlement resolving a yearslong investigation by his office and the U.S. Department of Justice into the hospital's gender care program for minors. The Houston hospital also agreed to terminate five physicians who previously provided transition care to children and to pay $10 million to settle allegations of improper Medicaid billing for such care. For the first five years of operation, the clinic must provide detransition services at no cost.

Patten said the settlement 'reflects an institutional and fundamental cultural shift away from radical gender ideology.' The hospital, for its part, said it agreed to settle to protect resources from 'endless and costly litigation,' maintaining it had followed all applicable laws throughout. The hospital produced more than 5 million documents over the course of the three-year investigation and conducted multiple internal reviews.

Details of what clinical services the detransition clinic will offer have not been released. Detransitioning — the process of no longer identifying as transgender or ceasing medical transition — is considered rare, and the medical interventions involved are largely similar to those used in transitioning, including mental health therapy and hormone treatment. Critics of the settlement argue it represents government coercion of a medical institution, while supporters contend it corrects inappropriate care provided to minors. The agreement marks a significant escalation in state and federal efforts to restrict gender-affirming care for children.

stories.headline: Colombia Presidential Campaign Manager Killed Two Weeks Before Election
stories.summary:
The local campaign manager for Colombian presidential candidate Abelardo de la Espriella and one of his aides were shot and killed late Friday, Colombian officials confirmed Saturday. The killings occurred approximately two weeks before Colombia's presidential election on May 31, which will determine the successor to President Gustavo Petro, the country's first leftist head of state.

The assassinations have intensified concerns about political violence in the run-up to the vote. Colombia has a long history of violence against political figures, particularly those challenging entrenched criminal and paramilitary networks. No group has immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

The May 31 election marks the end of Petro's term and is seen as a pivotal moment for the country's political direction. The killing of a candidate's regional organizer so close to election day raises alarms about the security environment surrounding the vote and the safety of campaign workers operating in areas with active armed group presence.

stories.headline: Gunmen Kidnap More Than 50 Children, Including Toddlers, From Nigerian Schools
stories.summary:
Armed gunmen abducted more than 50 children from three schools in Mussa, Borno state, in northeastern Nigeria on Friday, with most victims aged between two and five years old. Eyewitnesses told the BBC that the attackers used the children as human shields while fleeing on motorbikes, preventing security forces from opening fire. A statement from Senator Ali Ndume of Borno South confirmed at least 42 children were taken from two of the schools.

Headmaster Abdu Dunama of Mussa Central Primary School said armed men stormed the building after troops on patrol had departed the town, seizing 34 children — mostly nursery pupils aged five and under — directly from their classrooms. No group has immediately claimed responsibility, though residents and analysts noted the attacks bore hallmarks of Boko Haram, the Islamist militant group contesting the region with its rival faction, the Islamic State West Africa Province.

The kidnappings have prompted an urgent appeal from the largely farming community for government intervention. Security forces are reported to be on the ground tracking the abductors. The incident is the latest in a spate of mass abductions across Nigeria and deepens an already severe humanitarian crisis in Borno state, a region that has endured decades of Islamist insurgency.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Rejects Virginia Democrats' Bid to Restore Voter-Approved Congressional Map
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Friday declined an emergency request from Virginia Democrats to reinstate a voter-approved congressional redistricting map that the Virginia Supreme Court had struck down as unconstitutional. The high court issued its order without any noted dissent, dealing a decisive blow to a Democratic effort that had drawn more than $64 million in spending and was seen as a potential path to flipping four House seats ahead of November's midterm elections.

The Virginia Supreme Court had earlier ruled that the process leading to the referendum approving the new map was legally flawed. The U.S. Supreme Court's refusal to pause that ruling and allow time for a federal appeal effectively ends the redistricting fight and leaves in place existing congressional lines that favor Republicans. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger blasted the decision, accusing both courts of nullifying voters' choices.

The ruling is the latest development in a broader national mid-decade redistricting competition, accelerated by Republican-controlled legislatures redrawing maps in multiple states following a Supreme Court voting rights decision. Democrats had bet heavily on Virginia as a counterweight to GOP gains elsewhere. Republicans argued the Democratic map-drawing process violated state constitutional procedures, a position now upheld at every judicial level.

stories.headline: Car Rams Pedestrians in Italian City of Modena, Injuring Eight; Woman Loses Both Legs
stories.summary:
A car plowed into pedestrians on a main street in Modena, a city in northern Italy, on Saturday, injuring at least eight people, four of them critically, local authorities said. One woman was pinned against a shop window and required the amputation of both legs, according to Mayor Massimo Mezzetti. Victims were transported to hospitals in Modena and Bologna, with the most critical cases airlifted by helicopter.

The driver, a 31-year-old man born in Bergamo and raised in the Modena province, mounted the sidewalk and struck multiple people before crashing into a shop front. Witnesses reported he was carrying a knife but did not stab anyone. Bystanders intervened to detain the suspect until police arrived; he is now being questioned at police headquarters while authorities determine whether the act was deliberate, linked to substance use, or both.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the incident "extremely serious" and expressed solidarity with the victims, praising citizens who helped subdue the suspect. Mayor Mezzetti said that if the act proved intentional, it would be "even more serious." Investigators have not yet publicly characterized the incident as a terrorist attack, and the suspect's motive remains under investigation.

stories.headline: Update: US Brokers 45-Day Lebanon-Israel Ceasefire Extension as Israeli Strike Kills Six
stories.summary:
The United States announced Friday that Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a 45-day extension of their fragile ceasefire, following two days of negotiations in Washington. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said the two sides hoped the discussions would "advance lasting peace" and full mutual recognition of sovereignty, with a security track to be launched at the Pentagon on May 29.

The announcement came the same day Lebanon's health ministry reported that an Israeli air strike on the town of Harouf in southern Lebanon killed six people, including three paramedics, and critically wounded a fourth paramedic at a civil defence centre. Israel has not commented on the specific strike. Lebanon accused Israel of targeting civilians and medical personnel, which Israel denies, saying its operations are aimed at Hezbollah fighters and infrastructure.

The ceasefire, originally brokered by President Trump on April 16, has been violated almost daily, with Israel intensifying air and artillery strikes and Hezbollah continuing rocket and drone attacks into northern Israel. Israel says it is establishing a buffer zone in southern Lebanon to prevent future Hezbollah attacks. More than one million Lebanese — roughly one in five of the population — have been displaced since the conflict escalated.

Israel's Ambassador to the US called the Washington talks "frank and constructive," while Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said he hoped to mobilize Arab and international support for Lebanon's negotiating position. The state department said a political track of negotiations would reconvene in June.

stories.headline: Trump Targets Sen. Cassidy as Louisiana Republican Senate Primary Votes Saturday
stories.summary:
Louisiana's Republican Senate primary is taking place Saturday, with incumbent Sen. Bill Cassidy fighting for his political future against Rep. Julia Letlow, who is backed by President Donald Trump. Trump used social media on Saturday morning to call Cassidy "a disloyal disaster" and "a terrible guy," predicting he would "get CLOBBERED" while praising Letlow as "a winner."

Cassidy drew Trump's ire primarily for voting to convict him in his second impeachment trial following the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack, and for clashing with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over vaccine policy, even though Cassidy provided crucial support for Kennedy's Senate confirmation. A third candidate, state Treasurer John Fleming, is also in the race. If no candidate clears 50 percent of the vote, a runoff will be held June 27.

The race is widely seen as a test of Trump's ability to purge the Senate Republican caucus of members he views as disloyal. Cassidy's campaign is expected to have spent roughly $9.6 million on advertising, with a supporting super PAC adding $12.3 million — significantly outspending Letlow. Some Republican strategists say the race is statistically unlikely but no longer impossible for Cassidy to win.

The primary is also complicated by a recent Supreme Court ruling affecting the Voting Rights Act, which prompted Louisiana to delay House primaries to allow congressional district lines to be redrawn, potentially causing voter confusion on Saturday. The Senate seat is heavily favored to remain Republican in the November general election regardless of which candidate wins the primary.

stories.headline: London Deploys 4,000 Police as Right-Wing Rally and Nakba Day March Converge
stories.summary:
London's Metropolitan Police deployed approximately 4,000 officers on Saturday as two major competing protests converged in the British capital, raising significant concerns about potential unrest. Authorities described it as one of their busiest and most operationally complex days in recent years.

A right-wing rally and a Nakba Day march — marking the 78th anniversary of Palestinian displacement following the 1948 Arab-Israeli war — are taking place simultaneously, heightening tensions between demonstrators and the risk of confrontation. Police have warned both groups of strict conditions on their movements and behavior.

The heavy security presence reflects broader anxieties in Britain about public order following a series of far-right disturbances in 2025 that prompted emergency government action. Authorities have signaled a zero-tolerance approach to violence or intimidation from any quarter.

stories.headline: FBI Offers $200,000 Reward for Former Air Force Specialist Who Defected to Iran
stories.summary:
The FBI announced a $200,000 reward Wednesday for information leading to the capture and prosecution of Monica Elfriede Witt, a former U.S. Air Force counterintelligence specialist who defected to Iran in 2013 and was indicted in 2019 on espionage charges. Witt, 47, remains at large more than a decade after her defection.

Witt served in the Air Force from 1997 to 2008, where she was trained in the Farsi language and deployed on classified counterintelligence missions in the Middle East. She later worked as a Defense Department contractor before defecting following two all-expenses-paid trips to Iran that the Justice Department said promoted anti-Western propaganda. According to the indictment, she provided the Iranian government with sensitive national defense information and conducted research to help Iran target her former U.S. government colleagues.

The FBI's decision to renew attention to a case that is more than a decade old comes at a moment of heightened U.S.-Iran tensions, with the two countries having been in a state of conflict since late February. The bureau said it believes "during this critical moment in Iran's history, there is someone who knows something about her whereabouts." Witt had been warned by the FBI before her defection but told agents she would not share sensitive information if she returned to Iran.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Leaves Beijing with Boeing Deal Claim but No Confirmed Trade Breakthroughs
stories.summary:
President Trump departed Beijing following a two-day summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, declaring the talks "very successful" and claiming China had agreed to purchase 200 Boeing jets with a potential commitment for 750 more — a deal Boeing confirmed. Trump also said American farmers would benefit from Chinese purchases of "billions of dollars" in soybeans, though Beijing has not confirmed any specific trade agreements.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi confirmed Xi will visit the White House in September, and both sides agreed to establish a "Board of Trade" to manage the bilateral relationship without reopening tariff negotiations. Notably, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that he and Xi did not discuss tariffs at all during the summit, a claim that surprised many observers given the looming November expiration of the existing tariff truce.

The summit was defined by warm symbolism — Trump received an honor guard, a state banquet, and access to the exclusive compound where China's Communist Party leaders reside — but analysts noted the gap between the rhetoric and concrete outcomes. China's foreign ministry spokesman declined to confirm specific deals, saying only that both sides should implement the "important consensus" reached and work toward stability in bilateral trade.

The absence of formal breakthroughs on tariffs, rare earth exports, or Taiwan leaves significant uncertainty heading into the fall. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated he expected progress on a future investment mechanism, but the summit's legacy may hinge on whether Xi's White House visit in September produces more tangible agreements.

stories.headline: Update: Rescue Diver Dies Searching for Bodies of Five Italians Who Drowned in Maldives Caves
stories.summary:
A Maldivian rescue diver, Staff Sgt. Mohamed Mahdhee, died Saturday after losing consciousness while searching for the bodies of five Italian divers who perished in a cave-diving accident earlier in the week at Vaavu Atoll, approximately 100 kilometers south of the capital Malé. Mahdhee was pulled from the water unresponsive and later died in hospital, adding a sixth fatality to what is already considered the worst single diving accident in Maldivian history.

The five Italian victims included Monica Montefalcone, a professor of ecology at the University of Genoa, her daughter, two researchers, and a diving instructor who served as the group's boat operations manager. The team entered the water Thursday morning and never resurfaced. Only one body is believed to have been recovered so far, found at a depth of around 60 meters — double the 30-meter limit for recreational scuba diving in Maldivian waters.

Maldivian President Mohamed Muizzu traveled to the atoll Saturday to observe search operations, which authorities have described as extremely high-risk due to unfavorable weather conditions. Investigators have not yet explained why the Italian divers descended to such depths or entered the cave system.

Italy's foreign ministry confirmed that 20 other Italian nationals aboard the yacht from which the group departed are unharmed and receiving assistance from the Italian embassy in Colombo, Sri Lanka. The cause of the original accident remains under investigation.

stories.headline: Anti-Immigration AI Videos Targeting UK Audiences Traced to Overseas Operators in Sri Lanka, Iran, and Vietnam
stories.summary:
A BBC Panorama investigation has identified dozens of interconnected Facebook and Instagram accounts producing AI-generated anti-immigration videos about the United Kingdom that have amassed millions of views — while being operated by individuals based in Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, and elsewhere in Europe. One account, "Great British People," presents itself as a Yorkshire-based page and has garnered 1.3 million views for a recent video of an elderly white man lamenting his pension, but is run from Sri Lanka.

The videos feature fabricated scenes including the House of Commons filled with men in traditional Arab clothing supposedly imposing Sharia law, and fake interviews with women in hijabs discussing Islamization of the UK. Several accounts previously focused on American political content before pivoting to anti-immigration narratives about Britain. Some accounts also share content sympathetic to the Russian and Iranian governments, though direct state involvement is difficult to verify.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan, who has separately commissioned research into AI-generated images depicting London in decline, said some account operators are motivated purely by money while others appear to be backed by hostile states. Cambridge University social psychologist Prof. Sander van der Linden described the accounts as a "new evolution of influence operations," warning that exposure to large volumes of AI fakes causes people to distrust authentic material as well.

The investigation highlights the ease with which overseas actors can purchase UK-registered social media accounts and use inexpensive AI tools to manufacture seemingly domestic political content, posing a challenge for platform regulators and election authorities ahead of future votes.

stories.headline: Train Kills at Least Eight in Bangkok After Freight Locomotive Strikes Public Bus
stories.summary:
A collision between a freight train and a public bus killed at least eight people and injured 25 others in Bangkok on Saturday, triggering a fire that engulfed the bus and spread to nearby vehicles. Emergency services dispatched firefighters and rescue crews to the scene, where teams worked simultaneously to pull survivors from the wreckage and contain the blaze.

Authorities said the fire has since been brought under control, with crews working to cool the area, ventilate gas, and continue searching for additional victims. The cause of the collision is under investigation, and Thai officials have not yet indicated whether driver error, a signal failure, or mechanical issues were responsible.

The crash represents a significant mass casualty event in one of Southeast Asia's largest cities, with the death toll potentially subject to revision as search operations continue.

stories.headline: Israeli Settlers Attack Areas of Palestinian Self-Governance in West Bank
stories.summary:
Violent Israeli settler attacks in the West Bank have expanded beyond areas under direct Israeli military control, with settlers now targeting zones where Israel formally agreed to Palestinian self-governance under past accords. The escalation represents a significant shift in the scope and reach of settler violence, according to reporting drawing on 14 news outlets across the political spectrum.

Israeli government critics and Palestinian authorities argue the attacks undermine any remaining framework for a two-state solution and amount to a systematic effort to drive Palestinians from territory designated for their administration. Human rights organizations have documented an increase in such incidents over the past year, with some accusing Israeli security forces of failing to intervene.

Supporters of the current Israeli government contend that settler activity reflects legitimate security concerns in areas where Palestinian governance has failed to prevent terrorism, and that characterizing the violence as organized policy misrepresents what they describe as the actions of individuals. The Israeli government has condemned some specific violent acts while drawing criticism for not prosecuting perpetrators at higher rates.

The story carries heightened significance given ongoing U.S.-brokered discussions around Gaza and regional stability. The West Bank situation remains a parallel and complicating front in the broader Israeli-Palestinian conflict, with implications for diplomatic efforts involving the United States, European Union, and Arab states.

stories.headline: Update: Six Hantavirus-Exposed Cruise Passengers Begin Three-Week Quarantine in Australia
stories.summary:
Six passengers from the MV Hondius — a cruise ship at the center of a hantavirus outbreak — arrived in Australia on Friday and were transferred to the Bullsbrook quarantine facility near Perth for a mandatory three-week isolation period. The passengers, five Australians and one New Zealander, all tested negative for the virus before departing the Netherlands but remain under observation given the 42-day potential incubation period identified by the World Health Organization.

Australian Health Minister Mark Butler described the government's response as among the world's most stringent, contrasting it with procedures in the United States and most European countries, where returning passengers are spending only a few days in quarantine centers before being released to their homes. The Bullsbrook facility was originally built in 2022 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and had remained largely unused.

Three people among the 11 confirmed cases from the MV Hondius have died. The ship, which was traveling from Argentina to Antarctica and remote South Atlantic islands when the outbreak was identified, is now sailing back to the Netherlands for cleaning and disinfection. Authorities have not yet determined what precautions will govern the remainder of the full 42-day incubation window once the initial three-week quarantine ends.

The outbreak has drawn global attention to hantavirus, a rodent-borne illness that is not typically transmitted person-to-person but carries a significant mortality rate in severe cases. The CDC previously reported monitoring 41 people in the United States for potential exposure.

stories.headline: Wife of Active-Duty U.S. Army Soldier Released After Month in ICE Detention
stories.summary:
Deisy Rivera Ortega, the wife of Sgt. 1st Class Jose Serrano, an active-duty U.S. Army soldier, was released from federal immigration detention on Thursday after spending approximately one month in custody. Rivera Ortega had been arrested at an immigration office in El Paso, Texas, on April 14. Her release was confirmed by the office of Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.).

The case drew attention as one of several high-profile instances in which family members of U.S. military personnel have been detained in the course of broad immigration enforcement operations. Critics, including Democratic lawmakers and military family advocates, argued the detention of a service member's spouse was a damaging and counterproductive consequence of current enforcement priorities.

Administration supporters and immigration enforcement advocates have maintained that legal immigration status requirements apply uniformly and that the government must uphold immigration law regardless of a detainee's family connections, while noting that the release demonstrates the system's capacity to address individual cases through review.

The case adds to ongoing national debate over the scope and implementation of immigration enforcement under current federal policy, particularly as it affects people with direct ties to the U.S. military.

stories.headline: Update: Andy Burnham Moves Toward Formal Challenge to UK Prime Minister Starmer
stories.summary:
Andy Burnham, the Mayor of Greater Manchester, has identified a credible route to challenge Prime Minister Keir Starmer for the Labour Party leadership, according to reporting from the New York Times and Politico. While no formal challenge has yet been declared, Burnham's positioning marks a concrete escalation in the internal party crisis that erupted this week with the resignation of Health Secretary Wes Streeting.

The development is the latest in a week of significant political turbulence for the Starmer government, which has faced an open party rebellion and the departure of senior cabinet members. Burnham is widely seen as a potential figurehead for Labour's left and centrist dissenters who believe Starmer has lost the authority to govern effectively.

Starmer's allies have pushed back against suggestions of an imminent leadership contest, arguing that internal party rules make a successful challenge logistically difficult and that the prime minister retains the support of a majority of Labour MPs. They contend that external pressures, including economic headwinds and opposition attacks, are being exploited by rivals.

The UK political situation remains fluid. A formal leadership contest would require a significant threshold of parliamentary party nominations, and it is unclear whether Burnham or any other potential challenger currently has sufficient support to trigger one. The story continues to develop.
